newsitem.title: USA: Hussein meets Albright after hints of new US role.
newsitem.headline: Hussein meets Albright after hints of new US role.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Jordan's King Hussein discussed the fractured Middle East peace process on Wednesday, a day after the king and President Bill Clinton both hinted at a new U.S. role in the negotiations.

After a White House meeting with King Hussein on Tuesday, Clinton said he was "personally prepared to do anything I can" to get peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians back on track after a series of violent flareups.
And the king said later that the current crisis required "a more active U.S. role," according to The New York Times.

"Minds have to be put to work and heads need to be knocked together," the king said, according to Wednesday's New York Times. "The United States is in the position to be the arbiter and the partner of all concerned. But the United States should not be just the messenger. That's what a new phase means."

As Albright met with the king at a working lunch, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns turned aside repeated queries about whether this new phase might include meetings with Middle East leaders at Camp David, outside Washington.

"Obviously what we have in mind is using the influence of the United States and the leadership of the president and the secretary of state to ... help the Israelis and Palestinians overcome their differences," Burns told reporters.
A landmark peace accord between Israel and Egypt was forged in 1978 in meetings at Camp David, the U.S. presidential retreat in rural Maryland.
At the White House, presidential spokesman Michael McCurry brushed aside questions about a possible Middle East summit, saying he was unaware of plans for such a gathering "right now."
"We've explored a number of ideas on how we can get the parties to re-engage," McCurry said at a briefing. "I'm not aware of any plans for a summit," he said.
King Hussein was scheduled to meet later on Wednesday with Defence Secretary William Cohen.

Albright has engaged in telephone diplomacy over the last days, talking twice with Palestinian Authority Chairman Yasser Arafat and once with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday, Burns said.
Burns said he could not confirm reports that a new clamp-down on violence in the Gaza Strip and West Bank was under way, but said that would be desirable.

"Obviously, we'd like the Palestinian Authority to take determined, concrete efforts to crack down on those people in the West Bank, the Gaza Strip, perhaps even some in Jerusalem, who are bent on violence and terror and who are using that as a political tactic to achieve their narrow political objectives," Burns said.
Netanyahu will meet with Clinton in Washington on Monday, a visit Burns called "important ... particularly now that the peace negotiations are in such dire straits."

Netanyahu said Israel would not resume peacemaking as long as Palestinian bomb attacks continued. They were touched off by Israeli settlement construction. Netanyahu spoke hours after a gasoline bomb was thrown at an Israeli bus in the occupied West Bank, wounding 11 soldiers.
It was the third bombing that Israel blamed on Palestinians in two days, and followed a suicide bombing March 21 that killed four people, including the bomber.
